Hi Sam,
Re: 53A
Crossword puzzles may very well include verbs or adjectives that one rarely has occasion to see or use elsewhere, but CONJURE is the opposite case! As you note, it hasn't been in a puzzle for more than 30 years, but I hear and see it frequently IRL, notably about contemporary politics.

And I give Leslie Benson a pass for DJSET given the easy crosses and the chance to get CONJURE back in a grid.
To me, this Monday was FAIRANDSQUARE.

I have not done Monday's puzzle--I probably won't even crack it open until my lunch break on Monday--but I wanted to comment on "the Great Easening."

My solving schedule is different han most. I normally have mid-week days off, so more time to leisurely solve, and dabble on Wordplay, on a Tuesday or a Wednesday, when the puzzles are easier. Fridays and Saturdays, I will begin the puzzle during my lunch break, and sometimes complete it. Well, most times, I guess.

Am I a good solver, that I can finish a Saturday puzzle, and eat lunch, in a half hour--or is it that, by 12:30 pm, after seven hours of rush, my adrenaline is so high, my mind is racing so fast, that the entries just come?

This past Saturday, I solved the puzzle in . . . let us say x minutes. Darned quick. But--I've been working back, leisurely, through the archives, and a couple days ago, I solved a Saturday from 2018 in, well, 1.33x minutes. Also pretty quick. How far back until they become reliably tricky?

If anything, I've noticed that the early week puzzles from eight years ago aren't as easy as the ones today. Also, BRO was just [Sis]'s sibling.
I like that SKYDIVE is vertical and FAIRANDSQUARE is on the level. I think this puzzle is excellent.

THE makes up 7% of written English, and Polish doesn't even feature an equivalent - we have no articles. For us, it's mostly syntax that indicates whether we mean a specific or non-specific thing. 

I only learned EEYORE from these puzzles - Polish children get to know Kubuś Puchatek (Fluffy Little Jacob), Kłapouchy (Flappy-Ears), and Maleństwo (Little One) in Polish - can you figure out which of the English characters those are?

I was curious as to whether this terrific theme has been done before in the major crossword outlets, and the answer is no it hasn’t.  It has been a revealer once before (in the LA Times) with answers in squares as in today’s, but the word in each square was simply FAIR.  

So, today’s theme takes the concept a step farther, and high props to Leslie for coming up with it.

After filling in two squares and the revealer and grokking the theme, it was fun trying to guess the last two FAIR squares after a cross revealed two of its letters.

I loved the beauteous pair of C answers CAVORT and CONJURE.  And the moment I looked at ARARAT backwards and realized it begins “boom de ay”.

First rate theme, fun, plus enjoyable touches – a sweet Monday outing for me.  Thank you, Leslie, and I’m looking forward to the Monday you have in the queue!

Anyone who plans their day’s activities around the crossword entries should be careful about SKYDIVE: Yes, the clue would allow you to brag at the next national puzzle gathering that technically you went sky diving even if the plane was still on the ground - but be careful, because if you jump head first you could hurt your head.


I see a poor and square homophone appearance starting just below square 6: MENU for “fare and square”. And I didn’t even hurt my head, that’s just how mine works even on a good day.
Wonderful!  We need more from you, Leslie, and I look forward to your next.

I am so happy that the revealer answer was put in the middle of the grid and not at the end.  This gave me a chance to participate fully in the 2nd half of the puzzle.  Once I saw FAIR AND SQUARE, I went back and noticed EXPO and SOSO in the gray squares I'd already completed.  "Lovely!" I thought.  Two different meanings of FAIR.  And now I had a mission other than simply filling the rest of the grid.  What would the two other meanings of FAIR be and could they be expressed in 4 letters?

Got 'em both -- before continuing with my solve.

FAIR = Blond, which doesn't fit.  But PALE does.  And FAIR also = JUST.  Which fits.

And that's JUST what those two squares turned out to be.  Yay, me!  And Yay, Leslie, for giving me a fun chance to play along.  Hope others here did the same thing.  I'd bet my bottom dollar that Lewis did, for one.

Long time lurker, first time commenter: yesterday was my one-year streak for the crossword (and a tough one). A significant part of the fun is this comment section and guessing the vibe of the posts while puzzling (“too easy”, “I like it hard but this was horrible”, “what a grid” and variations on a good theme). I think my favorite comment a couple of weeks ago was when someone said of the 2300 puzzles under their belt, it was definitely a top-50 worst one. So precise 😂

I’ve been doing crosswords since around 2020, started trying later in the week ones around ‘23 and ‘24, and worked up the consistency to handle slogs and tough ones with patience and Wordplay as a last resort. I’m not perfect but I can clear most every grid now without lookups. I love the warmth towards everyone at different points of crosswording journeys, and think it’s helpful to share the years of time and reps (around 1,500 completed puzzles total now) it took before I could get to this streak. 

Here’s to one of my favorite corners of HUMANS on the internet and more years to come 🙂

More on our previous talk:  Mann has Hans listen to a concert early in his visit.  The program includes music from Carmen and Der Freischütz.  Both are prophetic, eh?  Years later he describes the powerful roar of the waterfall as "infernal".

I believe that Mann, like Joyce, intends to provide "enough tricks and traps to keep the professors busy for years".  Critics specializing in Nietzsche, Freud, Wagner, Russian literature, and Greek philosophy have pounced.  Just as in the old tale of six blind men and the elephant.

I don't believe in the "tired European society hurtling toward the brink of the Apocalypse".  The  Bourgeois burghers, like Hans' grandfather, leave decisions on war and peace to the aristocracy.  For me, the prophetic warning is that people are apt to support the nonsensical ramblings of a "personality" like Peeperkorn over the penetrating logical arguments of S and N.

Aargh!  I do know east from west.  Sorry about that.

Possibly hung up on last week's West is Best discussion.

@Al  in Pittsburgh

Ah, but everyone knows it’s the Southwest that’s Best [grin]. Yes, it’s been a lot of transatlantic back-and-forth lately. I’m trying to get my dad to come and stay with us for a few weeks or months instead, but no luck so far. 

My Woods translation doesn’t call the roar of the waterfall infernal, but I just reread the scene and there is Peeperkorn’s “sybaritic roguishness, a dancing hitch of the robes, the holy lewdness of the heathen priest.”  Yes, a critical mass of any human tribe or society will at some point fall under the spell of someone appealing to their basest instincts. Luckily, then you have midterm elections. I find Naptha more dangerous than Peeperkorn: When you add intellect and zealotry and subtract pacifism (or at least sloth), that’s when nations go to war, and not half-heartedly as they would with Peeperkorns at the helm. These are all gross generalizations, naturally—and very disjointed ones—but I’ve got a 1,500-character limit and serious jet lag. 

I missed the significance of the reference to Der Freischütz when first reading the novel, likely  because I’m unfamiliar with the opera. Speak of the devil, though—and opera, and “enough tricks and traps to keep the professors busy for years"—in The Master and Margarita, Bulgakov weaves in allusions to Gounod’s Faust so much that I stopped reading at some point and found the opera on YouTube.
